summary.text:
The £16m discount is the reason to read this. In July 2025 Hertfordshire prepaid £91m of commercial bank loans running at 4.46% for a redemption cost of £75m, and the report is explicit that part of it was negotiated — "negotiated an attractive discount margin with the lender". It is being amortised over ten years at £1.6m a year, with the loans refinanced through PWLB at 5.35% on a smaller principal.

That is the second large discount story in the library after Cherwell's £14.6m, and the more instructive one, because paragraph 8.12 states the difference precisely: PWLB repayment rates are non-negotiable, commercial lenders' are not. Cherwell took what the formula gave; Hertfordshire negotiated.

Their account of the High Needs deficit at 8.8–8.9 is the fullest we have read anywhere — £83m, 90% to be funded by the new Stability Grant contingent on DfE agreement, notification expected September 2026, override ending 1 April 2028.

A tenth LOBO call: £9.4m of £19.4m repaid in June 2025. And on their own numbers borrowing of £649.5m now sits above a liability benchmark of £598.2m, which they do not comment on.

officer.body:
Hi [OFFICER NAME],

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on the year-end report that went to Audit Committee on 24 July. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it.

A cross-check first. We hold 52 PWLB loans for Hertfordshire at a balance of £616.2m against the £624.3m in your paragraph 8.14, four months apart. Your restructuring arithmetic checks exactly too — £91m of principal less a £75m redemption cost is the £16m discount, and £16m over ten years is the £1.6m annual benefit.

That restructuring is why we wrote, and specifically paragraph 8.12. You set out the mechanism more clearly than any report we have read this year: PWLB repayment rates are non-negotiable and sit below gilt yields, while commercial lenders have flexibility to negotiate premature redemption terms. Then 8.13 shows what that is worth — £91m of bank debt at 4.46% redeemed for £75m, with the discount margin negotiated rather than taken as offered.

We read a great many of these reports and almost all of them treat early repayment as a single question with a single answer: is there a premium, and is it too big. Yours is the only one that separates the two markets and acts on the difference. For context on the other half of it, Cherwell took a £14.6m discount from the PWLB on a 50-year loan in the same period — but that was the formula giving what the formula gives, with nothing to negotiate. You are the worked example for the commercial side, and if we ever write that comparison up we would want to ask you first.

The reason it matters going forward is that the same conditions still hold. Your remaining commercial exposure is £25.1m, and on the DMO's premature repayment curve this afternoon, notice 314/26, your PWLB book is one of the most evenly balanced we have priced — 19 loans carrying about £14.2m of discount against 32 carrying about £9.8m of premium, netting to roughly £4.4m. That balance is itself informative: it means the book has been built across enough rate environments that there is no single direction to it. We compute this daily on the DMO's own formula and yours is at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis. Standard caveats and we mean them — we don't sell treasury products, we model no MRP or accounting treatment, and only the DMO can quote.

Two other things worth flagging.

Your paragraphs 8.8 and 8.9 on the High Needs deficit are the fullest account we have read anywhere: £83m at 31 March, 90% to be funded by the new Stability Grant contingent on DfE agreement of the SEND Reform Plan, notification expected September 2026 or February 2027 if amendments are needed, and the override ending 1 April 2028. We now hold the same fact pattern at Wiltshire, Worcestershire and Herefordshire, all borrowing short against a High Needs deficit and an awaited grant. Yours is the clearest statement of the timetable, and the September notification is a dated decision point that four counties we read are waiting on simultaneously.

And your PI4. Current borrowing of £649.5m now sits above the liability benchmark of £598.2m, where the budget forecast had both at £699.7m. The report does not comment on it. On CIPFA's framing that is the point at which the indicator starts saying something rather than confirming something — worth a line in the next report before someone else asks.

A tenth LOBO call for our file, incidentally: your £9.4m repaid in June after the lender proposed a rise. Every one of the ten we have picked up across the sector was refused or repaid. Oldham published being offered 6.70% and 7.67%; Wolverhampton 6.19% to 6.26%. Your remaining £10.0m is more likely to be tested than not.

On training, four fit Hertfordshire. Debt restructuring is the obvious one and yours would be the case study. PWLB break costs — mechanics & live calculator sits beside it. LOBO loans (legacy) for the £10.0m. And Liability Benchmark: using it in practice, given where PI4 has just gone. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
